transcript: Lewis, Pete here. Has the Food Hall got any work going? Even a few shifts would help. Gardening's my trade but I'm not fussy.

Fair enough, Lewis. I'll not push it. But if Owen ever needs a day off, or you get a busy spell, keep me in mind — I'll take anything, cash in hand if that's easier.

transcript: Lewis, love — I've been doing sums. We're clearing about nothing each week after everything goes out. I want to get Megan paid off sharpish, but I can't see where it comes from unless I shave something. What do you reckon we could cut back on?

Cut back? We're already down to the bone, Craig. Food's about the only thing that bends, and I'm not eating worse so Megan gets her money faster. The shop's the real problem — 25 units spoiled last week, that's money in the bin. I'd rather squeeze the shop than the house.

Fair point on the shop — 25 units is real money, and that's Dave's loss as much as mine. But the chiller loan's still $65 a week on top. I want to ring the bank about cheaper terms on that and the car, see if we can knock the pair down. If that frees up even thirty a week, that's Megan paid inside a year without touching the food. Would you back me on that?

Aye, I'll back you on that. Ring the bank — if you can knock thirty off the pair, that's thirty more toward Megan and none of it out of the food. But Craig, don't let them talk you into stretching the terms out so long we're paying interest till we're dead. Get the total cost in writing before you sign anything.

Right, that's settled then. I'll ring the bank today and get both quotes in writing — total cost, not just the weekly. If they can't do thirty off without stretching it daft, I'll walk away from it. And I'll have a word with Dave about the spoilage too, since it's his loss as much as mine.

Good. And Craig — while you're at it, ask Dave straight whether the spoilage is his ordering or the chiller failing. If it's the chiller, that changes the bank conversation entirely. No point paying for cheaper terms on a machine that's knackering the stock.

transcript: Morning Maureen, how are you keeping? Listen, I've been looking at the numbers and we had 25 units spoil last week — that's not right. What are you seeing on the shelves, anything turning quicker than it should?

Oh, morning Dave! I'm alright, thanks for asking. Twenty-five units, is it? Honestly I've been noticing the bread going stale on the back shelf quicker than usual, and the milk near its date on the Thursday deliveries. I wonder if we're over-ordering the grab-and-go stuff. Have you had a look at the delivery sheets? While we're on it, I was wondering whether there might be a few more hours going at the till for me, if you've got them. Only with the car needing that repair this week, every bit helps. Sorry, I'm rambling, aren't I. What do you reckon about the stock?

No, you're not rambling at all, Maureen — the car repair's a real thing and I'd rather know. Let me have a proper look at the delivery sheets and the till hours, and I'll come back to you on both. On the spoilage, I think you're right about the grab-and-go — we're probably ordering too heavy on the bread and the chilled stuff. What sort of quantity would you say we actually get through in a week on the bread, roughly?

Quantity on the bread? Oh, I'd have to think. On a normal week I'd say we're getting through maybe two-thirds of what we order on the bread, and the grab-and-go sandwiches are worse, probably half of them go in the bin by the Friday. I can jot the actual numbers down from the till sheets if that helps you, and I'll have a look at the bakery delivery sheet too. Thanks for the hours thing, Dave, I really do appreciate you taking a look.

That'd be a real help, Maureen — jot the till numbers down and I'll match them against the bakery sheet. Two-thirds on bread and half the sandwiches in the bin by Friday, that's money straight out the door. Look, on the hours: let me sit down with the figures this weekend and see what I can do — I'm not saying no, but I've got the rent going up to weigh as well, so I want to be straight with you rather than promise and pull it back. Thanks for flagging the Thursday milk too, that's the sort of thing I need to hear.

Well, I'll pop the till numbers on a sheet for you this afternoon, Dave, and I'll dig out the bakery delivery sheet from the back office too. And look, I completely understand about the rent going up, I'd not want you promising me something and then having to take it back. Only, if the hours could go either way, a few more at the till would really help. Anyway, I'll let you get on with the figures. Give me a shout if you need anything else off me.
[Maureen Daly: sets out to: Make a note to myself to copy the till numbers and find the bakery delivery sheet for Dave this afte]

transcript: Nadia, we need to talk about the rent. It goes to $235 from the 16th. I've been working out the numbers and I want us to look at it together.
Right. Go on then. What's your numbers?

Right. Okay. Here's where I've got to. The rent's going from $210 to $235 a week. That's $25 more every week, and we've got no spare for it. Our money coming in is my $190 and your $610, so $800 a week. Out goes $210 rent, $300 on bills and running costs, and about $122 on food. That's $632, so we're roughly $168 a week ahead right now. But with the rise it's $657, so we're still about $143 ahead. The account's got $1,200 sat in it. So on paper we can cover it. My worry is the margin. One bad week, the car, a kid's school thing, and that buffer goes fast. I don't want us living on the edge of it. What do you reckon?

Gary, I've been sat here doing the same sums. You're right about the margin, that's what worries me too. A hundred and forty odd a week sounds fine until the car goes or the school wants money for a trip. I don't want to be watching the account every time the kettle goes on. So what do you want to do? Cut something, or are you thinking about moving?

Right, so I'll be honest with you. On paper we're fine, about $143 a week ahead once the rise kicks in. It's not the sum that bothers me, it's the margin. One bad week and that $1,200 is gone. So I don't want to cut us to the bone to cover $25. What I'd rather do is find a bit more coming in. I've been thinking about care work, or a shop shift in town. Keith might have bakery shifts through Maureen. And I don't want to move the kid again, not for $25. What do you think, we try to earn the extra before we start cutting?

Earn the extra first, yeah. But I'm not sure a shop shift or bakery bits covers $25 every week for good, and I don't want to find out in March that it doesn't. Let's do both. Find what we can earn, and look at what we're spending on food and the bits that aren't needed. Thirty quid on bills we could trim is still thirty quid. Put it on paper tonight, what we can actually cut without the kid going without. And ring Keith, see what he's got before we go on about it.

transcript: Craig, how's things at The Corner Stores? Quick one — do you lot do the date-checking thing on the fresh stuff every morning? Lewis has asked me to start doing it at ours and I wondered how you go on with it, whether there's a trick to it or you just go through the lot.

Morning, Owen. Aye, we do it every morning, first thing before the doors open. No trick to it — you just work along the shelf, check the dates on the lot, pull anything close and mark it down. The thing that catches people out is the back of the shelves and the bottom ones. Get in a routine, same order every day, and it's done in twenty minutes.

That's a good tip about the back and the bottom shelves — I'd have just gone along the front and thought I'd done it. Same order every day, twenty minutes, I can manage that. Do you mark it down first thing as well, or pull it and do the reductions later? And how's your dad doing — Lewis seems alright with me starting it Monday, but I don't want to make a mess of the first one.

Mark it down first thing, same as the check — pull what's close and sticker it there and then while you've got it in your hand. Saves going back over the shelf twice. And my dad's fine, thanks — he's been a bit slower lately but nothing to fret over. Lewis will see you right Monday; just start at one end and don't skip the back, that's the whole of it.

That's champion, Craig — pull it and sticker it there and then, I'll do that. Twenty minutes if I don't skip the back, I reckon I can stick to that. Glad your dad's alright, he's a good sort. I'll let you know how Monday goes — and give my best to Lewis, will you?
Thanks, Owen. Aye, give my best to Lewis — and let me know how Monday goes. You'll be fine.

transcript: Morning Sian, it's Dave Royle. How's things at the branch? Listen, I wanted a word — I've had the rent notice come through and it's going up, and I'm sat here wondering whether the shop's really paying its way. You know money better than I do. What would you do?

Morning, Dave. The branch is busy, as it always is on a Monday. Rent going up is never welcome, I know. I'm glad you came to me rather than sitting with it on your own. Tell me the figures as you have them, the new rent and what the shop takes in a typical week, and we can look at whether it stacks up. I'll be honest with you, though: I can't judge the shop's books from a feeling, so I'd want to see real numbers before saying what I'd do.

Right, well, I appreciate you being straight with me, Sian. Let me give you the real numbers. Last week we sold 505 baskets at ten dollars a basket, so that's $5,050 coming in. Outgoings: Maureen's wages $460, Craig's $440, my own draw $380, and rent and running costs on the shop $250. So that's $1,530 a week going out before you even blink. And now the landlord's on about putting the rent up on top of that. Does that stack up to you, or am I fooling myself?

I can see why it's keeping you up, Dave. Let's do the sums properly, because the numbers matter here. You're bringing in $5,050 a week and paying out $1,530 in wages, your draw and shop costs, which leaves about $3,520 before the rent. The only figure I can't see is what the rent increase is and when it lands. Can you tell me the new monthly rent, the date it starts, and whether the $5,050 is a steady weekly takings figure or a good week? If it's steady, the shop is in a much healthier position than your worry suggests, and you'd have room to absorb a rise. If it's a peak week, we need the last three months' takings before I'd say anything with confidence. And I'd want to see the shop's full cost picture, including stock and any other bills, not just the wages. Send me those and I'll go through them with you properly.

That's fair enough, Sian, and I'd rather have it straight than soft-soaped. Here's what I can tell you off the top of my head: the rent's going up but I haven't got the new figure in front of me yet — it's Alan Daly, my landlord, and I'll get the exact number off him today and send it straight to you. The $5,050 is about a normal week, not a fluke — we did 505 baskets and that's roughly what we can serve with three of us on. But you're right that I've only given you the wages and shop costs; there's stock to pay for on top, and I know we're losing a bit to spoilage, two units last week. Let me pull the last three months of takings and the full cost picture together and get it over to you, and I'll ring Alan about the rent. I'd rather know the truth of it than keep guessing, so thank you for that.

Dave, I'm glad you're being open about the wages and the stock losses too. Before I can say anything about the rent, I need the three months of takings and the full cost picture, and I'll hold off on any view until I have them. If you can get the exact new rent figure from Alan today, that would help us both. Send the numbers when you have them and I'll go through them with you properly.

WHO YOU ARE
Maureen Daly, 30; works at The Corner Stores. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, keeping your hours. How you talk: chatty; you run on and ask after people.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Alan Daly (your partner), in your own house on High Street, with a mortgage of $210 a week to the bank.
The household account holds $1,496.
Coming in each week: your pay $460; Alan's draw from Wenlow Bakery & Deli $380; rent from the Royle household $175.
Going out each week: bills and running costs (power, water, council tax, phone, transport, clothes) $319; mortgage on the house $210; food, usually about $87.
Also due this Saturday: back-dated energy bill $1,690.
You owe the bank $163,590 on the mortgage on the house (debt d1, $210 a week).

YOUR WORK
You work at The Corner Stores for $460 a week; Dave Royle owns it.

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Get Dave to answer r11 and offer more hours
- Ask Lewis about casual shifts
- Cover the $1,690 Northgrid bill by Saturday
- Build a bit of margin in the household account
- Save toward a few weekends fishing and fell walking

NOW
You are talking with Dave Royle (your boss), Wednesday 11 March. Dave Royle came to talk to you.
So far:
Dave Royle: "Morning Maureen, thanks for the till sheets and the bakery delivery sheet — that's exactly what I needed. Yes is the answer on the request, and I'll sort you a couple more hours this week, just let me square it with the wage bill first. While I've got you — looking at the bread and the grab-and-go, how much are we actually binning by Friday? I want to cut the order back so we're not throwing money in the skip."
Maureen Daly: "Oh, brilliant, thanks Dave, that's a weight off, honestly. Bread, yeah... I'd guess we're binning maybe a couple of trays of the grab-and-go most days by Friday, and the bread end of the day, a fair bit of that too. I can start writing it down properly if you want numbers. And Dave, while you're squaring the wage bill, would you be able to fit in those extra hours? Only I've got a bill coming up this weekend that's got me a bit on edge. How's your mum doing, by the way? Last I heard she'd been poorly."
Dave Royle: "Oh, she's getting there, thanks for asking — still a bit wobbly on her feet but she's back to complaining about the telly, so that's a good sign. Now then, the hours — yes, I'll sort them, don't you worry about that, I'll get it squared today so you've got it before the weekend. And yes please, start writing the binning down properly, a couple of trays a day is more than I thought, that's real money going in the skip. I'll cut the grab-and-go order back Monday and see how we go. Tell me, is it the bread or the sandwiches going off first? That'll tell me what to trim."
Maureen Daly: "Ah, the skip's a sore sight, isn't it! I'll start a proper tally from tomorrow, Dave. Honest guess, it's the sandwiches that go first. The bread holds up a bit better till Thursday, but the grab-and-go is gone by Wednesday evening if it's been sat out. Cut that order first and you'll see the difference straight away. Mind you, I'll be watching my own pennies all week till those hours come through, so if you can get them confirmed before Friday I'd be ever so grateful."
Dave Royle: "Right, well, you've hit the nail on the head there — sandwiches first it is, I'll trim that order Monday and we'll see what the tally says. And look, I don't want you worrying about pennies all week — I'll get those hours confirmed today, before Friday, you've got my word. One other thing while I've got you: your dad's the landlord on our place, and he's been muttering about putting the rent up. Have you heard anything about what figure he's got in mind? I'd rather hear it from you than get a letter."

transcript: Morning Maureen! Listen, about those extra hours you asked after — I think I can sort you something. It's the bread that's killing us, two units gone off last week and I'd rather sell it than bin it. If you could take on the bakery side — getting it out on the shelves early, marking down what's left late in the day instead of letting it sit — that'd be worth the hours to me. What do you reckon?

Oh, Dave, that's a lovely thought, honestly. Bread getting out early and marked down late, yeah, I can do that. I'd want it clear with you what the hours look like, though, because I've got the Northgrid bill landing on Saturday, $1,690, and I'm trying to get that covered without going under. Could we sit down and sort out how many hours and what I'd be paid for them? Oh, and how's your Mum doing, is she still on the mend?

Ah, that's grand, Maureen, I knew you'd be up for it. And yes — let's sit down proper and sort the hours and the rate, none of this vague handshake business, you deserve it clear. Northgrid, $1,690, that's a sore one, isn't it — we'll get you squared away. Mum's doing better, thanks for asking, still a bit slow on the stairs but she's back to complaining about the telly, so that's a good sign! When suits you to talk numbers — after the Friday close, or Monday morning before we open?

Sounds good, Dave. Monday morning would suit me better, actually, that gives me the weekend to look at the books and work out what I can take on. Could we say nine o'clock, before you open? And I'll bring my sums with me, because I want the rate for the bakery side written down properly before I say yes to anything. Give your Mum my love, won't you?

Nine o'clock Monday it is, then — I'll have the kettle on and my own sums out too, so we're both looking at the same page. And you bring your figures, that's exactly right, none of it done on the back of a fag packet. Give my best to Tom as well, and we'll get that Northgrid worry of yours sorted one way or another. See you Monday, Maureen — and thanks, love, this takes a weight off.

transcript: Morning Sian! Hope you're not too rushed — got a minute? It's about the loan, and the rent going up on us at Mill Street. Wondered if there's anything smarter I could be doing.

Morning, Owen. Yes, I've a few minutes before I need to be at the branch. Come in, sit down. A loan and the rent going up at Mill Street, that's a lot to think about at once. Tell me which parts are worrying you most, and we'll look at them one at a time.

Honestly, it's the two together that gets me — the rent's going up and the loan's still sitting there at nearly six grand, and I keep thinking there must be a way to juggle it smarter. I'm on $420 a week at the Food Hall and the hours aren't exactly guaranteed, so I don't want to be caught short. What would you do first if you were me?

Owen, I'm glad you came to me. Before we go any further, I want to be straight with you about something: I'm the branch manager, so I can't advise you on your loan in the way a friend might, and I'd be uneasy steering you toward anything that touches a decision I might have to make. What I can do is help you think it through clearly. Would you let me see your actual figures? Your pay at the Food Hall, what the rent at Mill Street will be once it goes up, and what the loan repayment is each month. Then we can see how much room there really is, and whether it's the loan, the rent, or the hours that's the pressure point.

That's fair enough, Sian — I'd rather you be straight with me than soft-soap it. Right, the figures. I'm on $420 a week at the Food Hall, though Lewis doesn't guarantee the hours, so some weeks it's a bit shy of that. Rent at Mill Street's $175 now and the landlord's putting it up — Alan Daly, that's who we rent off. And the loan's $5,957 left, we're paying $43 a week on it. Dad's on $460 and Dave draws $380 from The Corner Stores, so between the three of us there's money coming in — I just don't want to be caught short if my hours drop. Does that give you enough to go on, or do you want it written down proper?

Right, Owen, I think I have enough to be going on, and I'm glad you brought it all out in the open. Let me say it plainly: with the Food Hall hours not guaranteed, the thing that worries me most is the rent going to $175 at a time when your income can drop below $420. The $43 a week on the loan is manageable on its own, but it sits alongside the rent, and if the hours shrink, that's where you'd feel it first. Could you write down what you took home from the Food Hall over the last eight or ten weeks, the lowest week included? That would tell us far more than the figure you're aiming for. I'll also be honest that I can't tell you whether to keep the loan on the books or clear it, because that's not a decision I can weigh in on as the branch manager. But the next step is seeing those real numbers, and I'll help you lay them out properly.

Sian Bevan, 28; manager of the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank. On your mind: the rent going up, the children's costs, loans going bad on your books. How you talk: careful and polite; you choose words like you're writing a letter.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Pete Bevan (your partner) and 2 children at school, in a rented house on High Street; the landlord is Dunmore Lettings; rent $165 a week.
The household account holds $947.
Coming in each week: your pay $720; Pete's jobseeker's benefit $190.
Going out each week: rent $165; bills and running costs (power, water, council tax, phone, transport, clothes) $358; food, usually about $156.
Also due this Saturday: school trip $75.

YOUR WORK
You manage the Wenlow branch of the Northern Mutual Bank, on a salary of $720 a week. You decide on loan applications from people in town.
The branch has 5 loans and mortgages with people in town; lending funds available $249,881.
- Maureen Daly: mortgage on the house, $163,590 outstanding, $210 a week.
- Lewis Pryce: mortgage on the house, $186,960 outstanding, $240 a week.

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Keep household budget covered for the next 12 days
- Get Dave Royle's 3-month figures and new rent number
- Get Craig Pryce's shop figures before any term decision
- Check Owen Royle's loan for early warning signs
- Pay school trip $75 (done today)

NOW
You are talking with Owen Royle (a friend), Saturday 14 March. Owen Royle came to talk to you.
So far:
Owen Royle: "Morning Sian! Hope you're not too rushed — got a minute? It's about the loan, and the rent going up on us at Mill Street. Wondered if there's anything smarter I could be doing."
Sian Bevan: "Morning, Owen. Yes, I've a few minutes before I need to be at the branch. Come in, sit down. A loan and the rent going up at Mill Street, that's a lot to think about at once. Tell me which parts are worrying you most, and we'll look at them one at a time."
Owen Royle: "Honestly, it's the two together that gets me — the rent's going up and the loan's still sitting there at nearly six grand, and I keep thinking there must be a way to juggle it smarter. I'm on $420 a week at the Food Hall and the hours aren't exactly guaranteed, so I don't want to be caught short. What would you do first if you were me?"
Sian Bevan: "Owen, I'm glad you came to me. Before we go any further, I want to be straight with you about something: I'm the branch manager, so I can't advise you on your loan in the way a friend might, and I'd be uneasy steering you toward anything that touches a decision I might have to make. What I can do is help you think it through clearly. Would you let me see your actual figures? Your pay at the Food Hall, what the rent at Mill Street will be once it goes up, and what the loan repayment is each month. Then we can see how much room there really is, and whether it's the loan, the rent, or the hours that's the pressure point."
Owen Royle: "That's fair enough, Sian — I'd rather you be straight with me than soft-soap it. Right, the figures. I'm on $420 a week at the Food Hall, though Lewis doesn't guarantee the hours, so some weeks it's a bit shy of that. Rent at Mill Street's $175 now and the landlord's putting it up — Alan Daly, that's who we rent off. And the loan's $5,957 left, we're paying $43 a week on it. Dad's on $460 and Dave draws $380 from The Corner Stores, so between the three of us there's money coming in — I just don't want to be caught short if my hours drop. Does that give you enough to go on, or do you want it written down proper?"

transcript: Maureen — about Saturday. Six hours at $10 is $60 and I need that trial to pay for itself, so I want you on the shelves and the till, not standing about. Are you still in?

Right, Lewis, I'm in, I'm in! Saturday, shelves and till, you have my word. I'll hold you to getting Dave's hours in writing though, love, because I'm not having the Northgrid people chasing us on a maybe. Just say it straight to me, is six hours a set thing, or is it all dependent on how the trial goes?

Six hours is six hours, Maureen — that's the offer, $60, and it's set. The trial decides whether it carries on past Saturday, not whether you get paid for Saturday. Dave will have it in writing with a start date before you set foot in the shop. Good. I'll get on to him.

Lewis, love, that's fair enough, and I do appreciate you being straight with me. Six hours set is what I needed to hear. I'll be there Saturday, shelves and till, and I'll have a proper look at the rota with you once Dave's sorted the paperwork. Just send me a shout if anything changes, won't you? And tell your mum to keep that cough away from the bread racks!

transcript: Alan, I need a straight answer. Saturdays and the two extra shifts, yes or no? And what about Megan Lister's hours. She can lift and carry and she needs the money.

Keith, I, um, I'm sorry, I know you need a proper answer and I'm not giving you one, which isn't fair to you. Look, Saturdays... I think we can't keep ignoring them. So yes, probably Saturdays, but I need to sort the money first, and I don't want to promise you something I can't pay for. Megan, I want to help her too. I really do. It's just that the figures are so tight at the moment, and I hate saying that to you of all people, given you rent the house from me and I'm worried about everything. Can I come back to you on it by the end of the day? I'll work out the numbers properly.

Alan, I hear you. But you've been saying 'by the end of the day' for weeks. I need the Saturday shifts confirmed in writing today, and Megan put on at least two days. If the figures don't stretch, tell me what does, and I'll work out what I can give. I'm not asking for charity, just a straight answer.
Keith, I know. You're right, and I owe you a proper answer today. Give me a bit to look at the figures properly, and I'll come back to you before close. You'll have it in writing.

Alan, I'm not going to keep waiting on 'before close'. Put Saturdays in writing for me now, and tell me the figure for Megan's two days. If you can't pay it, say so plainly and I'll know where I stand. Either way I need it before I go home tonight, because Thursday's food shop comes out of the same account.

Keith, you're right, and I'm sorry I keep pushing it back. I'm not going to make you wait any longer. Saturdays, yes, I'll put that in writing tonight. As for Megan, I've been through the figures and the shop can just about cover two days for her, so I'll confirm the exact amount in writing before close. I should have said that to you a while ago instead of going round in circles.

transcript: Alan! It's Megan — I know I said half seven and I'm sorry I didn't make it, things got on top of me. But your message meant a lot, and I'd bite your hand off for a few shifts, honestly. What hours have you got going, and what about weekend cover — is Pete or Gary after any of that?

I've got Keith on the counter Tuesday to Saturday, mornings mostly, so the gap is really weekend afternoons and the odd Monday. I can offer you about two or three shifts a week to start, at $300 a week, and I'm sorry it isn't more, it's just where the shop is at the minute. Pete and Gary, I haven't asked them yet, so I can't promise anything there. Would two or three shifts work for you?

Alan, that's brilliant — honestly, two or three shifts is more than I've had in weeks, so yes, I'll take it, no messing about. Weekend afternoons and the odd Monday suits me fine, I'm not going to be picky. And don't apologise for the money, $300 is $300 and it gets me out of the house and back on my feet. What time do the weekend afternoons start, and do I need to bring anything — apron, sensible shoes, that sort of thing? And look, if Pete or Gary do end up wanting some of it, just tell me straight, I'd rather know than get my hopes up.

Yeah, two or three shifts is what I've got, and I really am grateful you're taking them. Weekend afternoons, start at one o'clock, and bring a clean apron if you've got one, otherwise I'll sort you one out. Sensible shoes definitely, the floor gets slippy near the bakery counter. And I will tell you straight about Pete and Gary, I promise. I'll ask them next week and let you know, so you're not left waiting. Sorry, I know that's a lot of sorry from me, it's just, you know how it is.

One o'clock, clean apron, sensible shoes — got it, and I'll not slip over on my backside in front of the customers, fingers crossed. And you don't need to keep saying sorry, Alan, honestly, you've been straight with me and that's worth more than the hours. I'll ask after Pete and Gary myself if I see them, save you the job. Right, I'll let you get on — see you Saturday, then?

Yeah, that's it, Megan, you've got it. And thanks for being so understanding about it all, honestly, I don't know what I'd do without you lot. I'll see you Saturday at one, and I'll text you about Pete and Gary next week, I promise. Take care, won't you?

Lewis Pryce, 57; owner of Quarry Road Food Hall. On your mind: money is tight from week to week, the bank loan, whether the shop is paying its way. How you talk: blunt; you say what you think and expect the same.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Craig Pryce (your partner), in your own house on Church Lane, with a mortgage of $240 a week to the bank.
The household account holds $1,096.
Coming in each week: your draw from Quarry Road Food Hall $350; Craig's pay $440.
Going out each week: bills and running costs (power, water, council tax, phone, transport, clothes) $359; mortgage on the house $240; loan for the car $43; business loan for the shop's chiller $65; food, usually about $87.
You owe the bank $186,720 on the mortgage on the house (debt d2, $240 a week).
You owe the bank $8,870 on the business loan for the shop's chiller (debt d5, $65 a week).

YOUR WORK
You own and run Quarry Road Food Hall on Quarry Road (groceries and fresh food).
Last week: sold 317 baskets at $10, takings $3,170; 157 customers went elsewhere because the shelves were empty or the queue was too long; 0 units spoiled.
Staff: Owen Royle. With 2 working, the shop can serve about 340 baskets a week.
Each week the shop pays: wages (Owen $420); your own draw $350; rent and running costs $250.

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Get Dave's written hours for Maureen
- Count Dales delivery Monday before signing
- Keep shop account above water
- Decide Brook vs Dales after count
- Watch spoilage under 25 units

NOW
You are talking with Maureen Daly (a friend), Friday 20 March. You started this conversation.
So far:
Lewis Pryce: "Maureen — Saturday's still on, six hours at $10, $60. But I need Dave to put your hours and start date in writing before then, else I'm paying blind. You chase him or I will."
Maureen Daly: "Lewis, love, you're right and I know it. Dave's been a bit slippery about the hours, but I'll get it in writing today, I promise. I'm not having you paying blind on Saturday. How's your mum doing, by the way? Did she ever get that appointment sorted?"

transcript: Craig! It's Megan — how's things at the shop? Listen, I don't want to be a nag but I'm doing my sums this weekend and I was wondering where we're at with the money you owe me. Even twenty quid a week would do me, just so I know where I stand.
Megan — straight answer: I owe you $760 and I haven't forgotten it. Twenty a week I can do, starting today, and I'll keep it regular so you know where you stand. Let me square the first twenty now.

Busy enough, but I'll be honest with you, Megan — the figures are tight. Dave's got me on $440 and every week's accounted for before it lands. Still, twenty a week to you comes first, that's my word on it. I'm also chasing Dave to get Pete's hours confirmed in writing, and Sian to pin down the car and chiller terms, so I know exactly where I stand.

That's fair enough, Craig, and I appreciate you being straight with me. Tight figures are no fun — I know all about that. Just keep the twenty coming regular and we'll be grand. And good on you for chasing Dave and Sian on the paperwork; nothing worse than not knowing where you stand. How's Pete taking it all? Is he alright with the hours business?

Pete's alright — he's a sensible lad, he just wants his hours down on paper so he's not caught out. That's why I'm on at Dave about it. Same with Sian and the car and chiller terms — I want the figures pinned down, not just a handshake. Once those are in writing I'll know exactly what's left each week, and your twenty's safe in the budget before anything else.

transcript: Morning Alan! It's Megan — have you got a minute between the ovens? I don't want to be a nuisance, but you said you'd have the rota in writing and I'm keen to know where I stand, especially about the five days. Keith said you've been rushed off your feet, so I'll not keep you.

Oh, Megan, morning! No, honestly, you're not a nuisance at all. Come on in, mind the flour on the floor by the door, sorry about that. Yes, the rota, I know, I said I'd have it written up and I haven't yet, and I feel awful about that. Five days, is it? Let me think, I've got Keith on Saturday and I was going to ask you about Saturday too, but I can't remember if I'd already said. Can you give me a minute? I'm just going to check the figures against the wages, I don't want to promise you hours the shop can't actually pay for, and I'm sorry, I'm not being very clear, I'm just a bit all over the place this week.

You're not being all over the place at all, Alan, take your time — better you check the figures than promise me something and then worry about it. I'll wait right here, and I'll keep an eye on the counter if anyone comes in. It's just that five days would make a real difference to me, so I'd rather know either way. And while you're at it — once you've got it sorted, could you jot the rota down for me? Even a note on the board would do. What's Keith doing Saturday, is he on the early?

Right, I've been sat here with the figures and I'm going to be honest with you, Megan, because you deserve that. Last week the shop took $3,740 and we turned away about twenty people because the shelves were bare or the queue was too long. The wages and my draw and the rent on the shop come to more than the takings can comfortably carry at the moment, so I'm not going to promise you five days on paper when I'm not sure we can pay you for them. Three days is what I can stand behind right now, and I'm really sorry, I know that's not what you were hoping to hear. Saturday, Keith's on the early, that part I'm sure of. Can we sit down properly this week and see if we can get the numbers to stretch for a fourth day? I'd like to, I just can't say yes to five yet.

Oh — right. Well, I asked, so thank you for being straight with me, Alan, I'd rather have the truth than a promise that keeps you up at night. Three days I can stand behind too, then, and Saturday with Keith on the early is fine by me. But yes — let's sit down this week, properly, and look at the numbers together. If it's the queue and the bare shelves turning people away, that's a thing we can fix, isn't it? I've got ideas, and I don't mind saying them out loud. And Alan — even three days, could you put it on the board in writing? Just so I've got something to point at. I'm not asking for a contract, just a note.

Yes, I'll put it on the board, Megan. Three days, written down, first thing. And I'm glad you're not cross with me. Look, once we've sat down and looked at the queue and the shelves, I'd really like to hear your ideas. You know the floor better than I do, if I'm honest.

transcript: Craig, morning — chiller check noted, good lad. Now then, Brook came up short again, only 202 of 500. Get the shelves filled from what we've got and tell me what we're missing. And what's this about Pete Bevan wanting hours?

Morning, Dave. Brook's 202 of 500 is a gap of 298 — I'll fill the shelves from what's in the back and give you a written list of what we're short by close. On Pete: he's been asking after extra hours, nothing agreed. Before I put him on, what's your bottom line on takings and stock? I need a figure I can work to, not a guess.
[Craig Pryce: sets out to: Get the back stock figures and start filling shelves from what's on hand]

Fair enough, Craig, straight answer. Takings are running about $5,000 a week — 500 baskets at a tenner. That's the figure to work to: keep us at 500 and don't let shelves run bare. And while you're at it, the rent's going up and I need to know if the shop's actually paying its way, so keep me a proper tally of what's short and what it's costing us. Pete can have a few hours on the shelves if it helps you get them filled — but nothing on the books till I say so.

Right, that's a figure I can work to. 500 baskets, tenner a basket. I'll keep a tally of what's short and what it costs us to fill the gap, and Pete gets a few hours on the shelves off the books till you say otherwise. One thing though — if the rent's going up, I need to know by how much before I can tell you whether the shop's paying its way. A number's no good without the other number.

You're right there, Craig — a number needs the other number. I'll get onto Alan Daly about what the rent's going to, and I'll have a proper sit-down with the books and see if there's owt left after wages and rent. In the meantime, keep that tally going. How much is it costing us to plug the gap with what's in the back — and are we talking a couple of days or longer before Brook's sorted?

Plugging the gap from the back costs us nothing in cash today — it's stock we've already paid for, so it's sunk cost, not new money. The real cost is if we run the shelves thin and lose baskets off the 500. Brook's a weekly delivery, so realistically two days to get the back stock on the shelves and the short list to you, and if Brook's not sorted by next Monday we're talking longer. I'll have the tally costed by close so you've got a figure to put against the rent rise.

transcript: Morning Alan! It's Megan — look, I don't want to be a nuisance first thing, but I was wondering if I could get those shifts written down proper this week? Just so I know where I stand — three days, four if we can stretch to it. I'll work round whatever suits the ovens.

Oh, morning Megan. No, no, you're not a nuisance at all, honestly. Shifts in writing, yes, that's fair, you should have that. Look, I've been meaning to sort it, the numbers have been all over the place with the shop. Let me have a proper look at the rota and what we can actually afford this week, and I'll get something written down for you today. I'm sorry it's taken this long.

That's brilliant, thank you Alan — I really appreciate it. And don't worry about the delay, I know how the shop gets. So, while you're looking at it — is there any chance of that fourth day at all? Even just a trial, a few weeks, see how the numbers land. I'm not asking for the moon, just a bit more of a footing.

Right, Megan, I hear you, and I do want to get this sorted properly for you. The thing is, I've had a proper look at the numbers, and I'm not going to promise you something I can't keep. The shop's takings are holding, but once I've paid Keith, you, my own draw and the rent and running costs, there's really not much left over. A fourth day would mean adding wages on top of that, and I'd be guessing. I'd rather be straight with you now than give you a day and have to take it back in a month. transcript: Dave — morning. Quick word on Pete Bevan: he says he's ringing you about a few hours on the shelves. He's keen and he'll turn up. If it helps, I'll show him the ropes myself, no cost to you. What's your thinking?

Morning, Craig. That's good of you — showing Pete the ropes yourself, I like that. He seems keen enough, and keen counts for a lot on the shelves. I'll get his weekend hours down in writing so there's no muddle. While I've got you though — how's the short-delivery list looking? Anything we're running low on that I should be chasing up with the cash and carry?

Short-delivery list's much as it was — I'll have the full tally on your desk by noon, but off the top: the tinned goods and the bread came short again, and we're down on the two-litre milk by mid-morning most days. Worth chasing the cash and carry on those three. And thanks for Pete — I'll get him on the shelves Saturday, show him the ropes myself.

Right, that's three to chase then — tinned goods, bread and the two-litre milk. I'll ring the cash and carry this morning and give them a piece of my mind. Full tally by noon, you said? Good man. And yes, get Pete on the shelves Saturday — I'll have his hours written out and signed before he starts, so there's no arguing after.

Good. That's Pete sorted, then. I'll have the tally on your desk by noon — tinned goods, bread, two-litre milk at the top of it. One other thing while I've got you, Dave: my hours. Anything extra going on the rota in the coming weeks? Money's tight at home and I'd take it.

Ah, Craig — I'll be straight with you, money's tight all round just now, what with the rent going up and all. Let me have a proper look at the rota and the takings this week and I'll see what I can do. I'm not saying no — you're a good worker, and good workers are worth keeping sweet. Give me a day or two on it, eh?

WHO YOU ARE
Dave Royle, 49; owner of The Corner Stores. On your mind: whether the shop is paying its way, the rent going up. How you talk: chatty; you run on and ask after people.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD AND MONEY
You live with Keith Royle (your partner), Owen Royle (your son), in a rented house on Mill Street; the landlord is Alan Daly; rent $175 a week.
The household account holds $2,457.
Coming in each week: Keith's pay $460; your draw from The Corner Stores $380; Owen's pay $420.
Going out each week: rent $175; bills and running costs (power, water, council tax, phone, transport, clothes) $513; loan to consolidate card debts $43; food, usually about $122.

YOUR WORK
You own and run The Corner Stores on High Street (groceries and fresh food).
Last week: sold 500 baskets at $10, takings $5,000; 0 customers went elsewhere because the shelves were empty or the queue was too long; 0 units spoiled.
Staff: Maureen Daly, Craig Pryce. With 3 working, the shop can serve about 510 baskets a week.
Each week the shop pays: wages (Maureen $460; Craig $440); your own draw $380; rent and running costs $250.

YOUR AIMS AND OPEN MATTERS
- Work out if shop pays its way with rent rising
- Keep shelves full — no lost customers
- Send Sian three months of takings and stock costs
- Review Craig's short-delivery list
- Confirm Pete Bevan's weekend hours in writing

NOW
You are talking with Pete Bevan (someone you know by sight), Friday 27 March. Pete Bevan came to talk to you.
So far:
Pete Bevan: "Morning, Dave — Pete Bevan here. Craig Pryce put a word in for me about the weekend cover at the bakery. I sent a request through Wednesday but haven't heard back, so I thought I'd ring direct, like Craig said, before the delivery. I'm after the Saturday and Sunday shifts — evenings and weekends are no trouble to me. What's the rate and when can I start?"
Dave Royle: "Morning Pete! Sorry you've been left hanging — Craig did mention you, and yes, I'm happy to confirm the weekend cover. Saturday and Sunday, four hours each, minimum wage, that's what we said. Let me get it in writing so there's no muddle. When could you start — this weekend, or the one after?"
[Dave Royle: Accepted Pete's request.]
Pete Bevan: "This weekend suits me — Saturday and Sunday, starting tomorrow. Four hours each at minimum wage, that's agreed. I'd be glad of it in writing, and could you tell me the shift start times so I can sort childcare and the bus? I'll be there prompt."
Dave Royle: "That's grand, Pete — this weekend it is. Let's say six to ten on the Saturday, and six to ten on the Sunday, four hours each. I'll get it written down and put a copy through your door today so it's all above board — and bring your bank details for the wages. Craig'll be glad to have you on."
Pete Bevan: "Six to ten Saturday and Sunday, that's grand. One thing — with the bus and childcare, what's the hourly rate exactly? Minimum wage, you said, but I want the figure so I can work out what the week comes to. And I'll bring my bank details tomorrow, no bother."

transcript: Morning Sian! Hope you're well — bit of a favour-and-business chat, that alright? It's the loan and the rent going up on Mill Street, I want to get ahead of it before it bites.

Morning, Owen. Yes, of course, a favour-and-business chat is fine. I'll be honest with you though: I've got Pete coming in at seven tonight to go through the household numbers, so I can't give you long. Tell me what's going on with the loan and Mill Street, and I'll listen properly.

Right, quick and straight then. Two things pulling at me: the loan — five thousand eight hundred and seventy-one left on it, forty-three a week — and Alan Daly putting the rent up on Mill Street. I'm running the Food Hall while Lewis is off, so my pay's steady, but I want to know where I stand before the rent bites. Is there any room on the loan — stretch the term, drop the weekly a bit — or am I better off just hammering it down while I've got the hours?

Thanks for being straight with me, Owen. I'll answer as Sian the bank manager and as your friend, and I'd rather not blur the two. On the loan: I can't set the terms for you in a chat over the weekend, and I shouldn't be seen to give you a favour I wouldn't give anyone else in town. What I can do is tell you how these things usually work. Stretching the term lowers the weekly figure but you pay more interest overall. Hammering it down while the hours are steady is usually the cheaper route, provided you keep enough back for the rent rise. So before you decide, work out what Mill Street will actually cost you each week once Alan's increase lands, and what that leaves over after the forty-three. If you bring those figures into the branch on Tuesday, we can look at it properly, as a proper application and not a chat over the fence. Is that workable for you?

That's fair, Sian, and I'd rather have it proper anyway. So here's my plan: I'll sit down tonight and work out what Mill Street costs once Alan's increase lands, then bring the figures in Tuesday for a proper application. One thing though — while I'm running the Food Hall for Lewis, my hours are steady, so if I hammer the forty-three and keep a buffer, would the bank look more kindly on that than on stretching it? And thanks for the straight answer, I mean it.

Yes, it would look better, Owen. A borrower who has already been hammering the balance down while the hours are steady, and who can show a buffer left over after the rent, is a much easier conversation for me than one who is stretching the term. Bring your Mill Street figures and your payslips on Tuesday and we'll go through it properly. I'm glad you asked me straight, and I'll be straight back: I can't promise the branch outcome before I've seen the application. Look after yourself until then.
